mappings.note: the statement to examine is that nationalism itself changed character after 1871, which is LO-3's 'evolution of the idea'; LO-4 was considered and rejected because the question is about the creed, not about what caused the war
the Habsburg patchwork at 5 marks with examples: the dynastic empire against which the nation state is defined, argued rather than listed. Same reading as the short version of this question
the cultural route to nationalism - Romanticism, folk song, language, Grimm's tales - is the cultural movement of LO-2; the question asks how it worked, so no recall competency

the four reasons the Balkans became Europe's flashpoint after 1871 - ethnic variety, Ottoman decline, mutual rivalry, great-power competition. LO-4 is literally an outcome about weighing reasons, so it stands alone
five named reforms Napoleon carried into the conquered regions; LO-1 content asked as a counted list, which is what separates it from the 'how did people react' items that take LO-1 alone
England's gradual nationalism set against the rest of Europe: a comparison of how states were made, LO-3, constructed by the student

similarities between the German and Italian unifications - fragmentation, Napoleon's indirect push, the 1815 reaction, the leading state; the mirror of the dissimilarities item and equally a constructed comparison

Polish nationalism kept alive through language, the Church and music after the partitions: a movement that never produced a state in this period, so LO-2 rather than LO-3, which is written around states that were formed
second wording of the culture-and-nationalism question; same LO-2 cultural-movement reading, since the two items test the same thing
the Greek movement traced through to the treaty and independence, so unlike Poland it is a movement that produced a state and goes to LO-3; 'discuss the characteristics' makes it a recounted list
the German unification narrated as a process, from the thirty-nine states through Bismarck's wars to 1871; the process items take LO-3 alone, the who-did-what items take LO-3 plus C-1.1

Renan's essay supplied as a source and questioned: the definition of a nation is LO-3, and working from an extract put in front of the student is C-1.2, the competency for applying knowledge to a new situation
the Civil Code extract and its export to the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany: LO-1 content read out of a supplied source, hence C-1.2
an extract on liberalism and the conservatism that followed Napoleon's defeat; both are isms (LO-2) and the answers must be drawn from the passage, so C-1.2

the extract is about what it meant to be a revolutionary and about Mazzini's Carbonari, Young Italy and Young Europe - the secret-society strand of LO-2, not Mazzini the unifier - read from a supplied source
the longer Renan extract, with the daily plebiscite and the modern-state contrast; same LO-3 subject as the other Renan case study, again answered out of the passage

Carl Welcker's argument against equality for women, supplied verbatim: the woman question inside the liberal movement (LO-2), with the student reading a hostile source rather than recalling the textbook line
one extract carrying both Romanticism and the economic hardship of the 1830s, which are the two halves of LO-2's 'diverse social movements'; a single outcome covers it, so no second content code
the extract on kingdoms, duchies, cantons and the Habsburg patchwork before nation states existed: LO-3's necessary starting point, answered from the passage
